summary: The concrete blocker is the transient npm/npx dependency-resolution path, not DSH profile loading or dsh-vision runtime code. On Windows 10.0.22631 x64 with Node 24.18.1 and npm 11.16.0, exact `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.1-rc.1 web` remained inside npm Arborist ideal-tree construction with no CLI output or listener for 180-300 seconds in both the normal environment and a clean isolated DSH_HOME/cache. In the controlled A/B, pnpm 11.7.0 resolved and installed the same exact top-level DSH package in 74.6 seconds; the installed DSH then reached HTTP 200 with both an empty DSH_HOME and the unchanged real profile, and the exact npx command reached HTTP 200 in 9.173 seconds when it could reuse that local installation. Confidence is high that npm/npx transient resolution is causal. A durable arbitrary-directory npx repair requires an upstream DSH packaging/dependency-locking or npm resolver change outside dsh-vision ownership, so no dsh-vision source fix was made.

The server was not misclassified merely for remaining alive: readiness was polled by HTTP and never observed.

tests.name: bounded clean temporary DSH_HOME startup probe for exact @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.1-rc.1 web using an isolated npm cache
tests.evidence: A newly created empty DSH_HOME and empty npm cache behaved the same: no stdout/stderr and no HTTP listener for 300.006 seconds. The isolated npm debug log showed successful registry GETs followed by npm Arborist `idealTree buildDeps` / `placeDep` work; it never reached package extraction or DSH execution before the bounded termination. This A/B rejects the real profile as the initiating cause.

tests.name: npm resolution/acquisition boundary and competing-hypothesis A/B probes
tests.evidence: Top-level rc.1 registry metadata returned successfully. A publish-time cutoff that excluded all rc.2 internal packages still timed out at 240.499 seconds; temporary npm 10.9.9 still timed out at 240.189 seconds; an empty working directory outside the repository workspace still timed out at 240.261 seconds. Thus rc.2 drift, npm 11 alone, and repository workspace context were rejected. In contrast, pnpm 11.7.0 resolved 504 packages and installed exact top-level rc.1 in 74.6 seconds, proving registry acquisition and the package graph were reachable through an alternate resolver.

tests.name: direct installed-package startup with clean and real DSH state
tests.evidence: The pnpm-resolved exact rc.1 binary reached HTTP 200 in 8.620 seconds with an empty DSH_HOME and in 5.630 seconds with the unchanged real DSH_HOME. The real profile contained the official base/web-app bundles plus @ran-sh/dsh-crew, no dsh-vision/image-mind bundle, and an empty cordis.patch.yml overlay. A minimal temporary profile without the crew layer also reached HTTP 200 in 8.256 seconds. Both the presence and absence of crew passed, rejecting crew/profile loading as causal.

tests.name: controlled startup probes against temporary copies with suspected layers varied one factor at a time
tests.evidence: The reliable minimal temporary-profile variation (official base/web-app only, crew removed, empty patch) passed in 8.256 seconds, while the unchanged real profile including crew passed in 5.630 seconds. No dsh-vision layer existed to remove. A byte-for-byte recursive copy attempt was stopped because copying pnpm-linked node_modules was slow and did not preserve equivalent link semantics; it was not used as evidence. Clean-home npx had already failed before DSH configuration loading, so binary profile isolation was not the causal branch.

The historical dsh-vision mutator is real but is not the present startup cause because the real patch is empty and the real profile starts when npm resolution is bypassed.

tests.name: post-remediation exact @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.1-rc.1 npx web probe in the intended real environment
tests.evidence: After exact rc.1 was safely pre-resolved in an isolated launcher directory without modifying DSH_HOME, the original system npm 11 exact npx command reused the local package, loaded the real profile, printed `dsh web: http://127.0.0.1:<dedicated-port>`, and returned HTTP 200 in 9.173 seconds. The probe then terminated only its own process tree. This proves the runtime/profile path works once transient npm resolution is removed. The launcher directory was diagnostic and was deleted; a durable arbitrary-directory npx fix remains upstream.

blockers: A durable fix for exact npx startup from an arbitrary directory is outside dsh-vision ownership. The minimum upstream follow-up is for @deepseek-ai/dsh to make the rc dependency closure deterministic (for example exact internal prerelease versions plus a validated lock/install strategy) and/or for npm Arborist to address the observed ideal-tree construction stall on this approximately 500-package graph. Until then, a locally pre-resolved exact package or pnpm-based launcher avoids the failing transient npm path without touching the official profile.
notes: Issue #13 and Issue #21 were read before diagnosis. Their separation between startup/profile investigation and later real-provider work was preserved.

Causal conclusion in plain language: npx is waiting in npm's dependency-tree construction before DSH starts. Removing the npx transient install step flips failure to success; changing DSH_HOME/profile contents does not. Confidence: high.

The rc.2 publication race was investigated but rejected: rc.1 declares 54 caret-based internal dependency ranges and normally selected many rc.2 packages after rc.2 was published, but a cutoff forcing rc.1-only resolution still stalled at the same npm phase.

No dsh-vision implementation fix or regression test was appropriate because no dsh-vision code ran on the failing path. No files were written in dsh-crew. Diagnostic caches, package trees, profile copies, and logs were deleted and were not committed.

The result is PARTIAL rather than PASS because the concrete cause and safe working A/B were proven, and exact npx reached readiness after local pre-resolution, but the upstream arbitrary-directory npx defect could not be durably repaired inside the authorized repository.
